agree.reason: The plain A1C numbers and $59 trial would build some trust with a wary reader, but someone who has quit three services before gets no word on no-contract cancellation, weekly swaps, menu variety or the call with the dietitian, so they have little reason to think this one will last.

honest.reason: The page drops the 'will lower your A1C' promise, reports 10/3/1 accurately and says medication changes aren't tracked, but 'people stay because the food is good' is an invented reason, and the unfilled order deadline leaves a blank where a fact should be.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out $12.90 a meal but leaves the most useful figures uncalculated: about 42% of customers have stayed past six months, 10 of 14 is about 71%, and the trial costs $5.90 a meal.

right_comparison.reason: It compares the service to planning and cooking yourself or ordering takeout, but never to what this reader actually tried and quit: apps and other delivery services.

qualification.reason: The A1C hedge is honest and names the confounders, but it gives the reader nothing to check, such as retesting A1C at three months or a way to judge the trial week.

objections.reason: The doubt about health promises is handled well, but the reader's main worry, quitting again, goes unanswered even though the facts that answer it (no contract, skip or cancel any time, 6 swap choices, a 4-week menu, a 15-minute call) were available.

fit.reason: It is a sales page of about the requested 400 words with a clear call to action, but it leaves out the service's name and the dietitian's name, and the order deadline is still a placeholder.
